rv.q: We all wanted to know if she's as good live on stage as she is on screen. And the answer is no: she's better.

'But her abrupt disintegration into fevered, ashen-faced confusion is seriously distressing. Although her performance runs a stunning gamut from cocky joy to despair and humiliation, it’s the subject matter that dominates the evening.' Arifa Akbar writes: 'Jodie Comer’s West End stage debut is a baptism of fire by any standards.
Comer is spry, sleek and smart, winning the audience over with her effervescent presence in Justin Martin’s staging.

She is nothing short of extraordinary as Tessa, the confident young barrister who starts the show by confiding in us the tactics she uses to wrong-foot witnesses and her overriding faith in the legal system to deliver justice.
Her performance, running a full-pelt 100 minutes, propels her into the front rank of stage stars.
If it's a great case study rather than a great play exactly, the cumulative effect is still quite something.
The argument is strongly made and forcefully delivered, though not all of it requires Comer's skill.
Comer manages to infuse breath-taking emotional drama in every last word.
Comer's performance is extraordinary, though, and Prima Facie is worth seeing for that alone.
It’s a personal triumph somewhat mitigated by the fact that the play she’s chosen is pretty clunky.

Comer’s performance is just so wonderful, capturing the comedic tones in the early scenes presenting the cocky, all-conquering female barrister who is a little too comfortable in herself and what she does.
It is flecked with humour and heartbreak brought to life by Comer’s adept delivery and commanding ownership of the stage under the Justin Martin’s assured direction.
Prima Facie draws vitally from Comer’s breathtaking performance in delivering its unique punches.
This production hits home, that is thanks to Jodie Comer’s performance which is earning standing ovations, and rightly.
Besides, Comer herself makes this unmissable viewing.
She brings its arguments to forceful life and in the process creates an unforgettable moment of theatre.
The fantastic news is that Comer's star power is entirely and utterly justified.
What a pity Suzie Miller’s monologue at this point falls apart too.

cn.t: Comer delivers an astonishing, tour-de-force West End debut in this powerful monologue about sexual assault and the legal system, though some critics find Miller's script overly polemical or structurally flawed in its second half.
